# What Git is {#sec-overview .unnumbered}

Git keeps the history of a project as a chain of snapshots, the commits. A
commit records every file of the project as it was at one moment, who made it,
when, and why, and which commit came before it. Its name is a hash of all of
that, so a commit never changes, and its name stands for the whole history that
leads to it. Branches and tags are names for commits: a branch moves on with
every new commit, and a tag stays where it was put. Every copy of a repository
holds the whole history, and copies exchange commits only when told to. Almost
everything that surprises newcomers follows from that: changes missing from a
commit, commits that seem lost, pushes that are rejected, and a history that
someone rewrote (@sec-model). Working with Git comes down to a few dozen
commands (@sec-usage).

For research software, the name of a commit is what makes a result traceable:
it says exactly which code computed the result, and a tag gives the commit of a
release a name that others can cite
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-traceability)). [](github-actions.qmd)
runs the tests on every commit pushed to GitHub.

The rule of this document, on what a commit should hold (@sec-atomic), uses the
[normative language](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-normative) of *Design
Principles*.

Checked against Git 2.56.


# At a glance {#sec-at-a-glance .unnumbered}

Every rule of this document in one line. The number and the title link to the
rule.

::: {.glance}
| No. | Rule | In one line |
|-----|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| [-@sec-atomic] | [](#sec-atomic) | Make each commit one change that leaves the project working, and keep refactoring, changes of results, and formatting in commits of their own. |
:::


# How Git thinks {#sec-model}

A repository is the directory `.git` at the top of a project, next to the files
you work on. It holds the commits, each of which points to the one before it,
its parent, and the names that point to commits (@fig-commits). Everything Git
does either adds commits or moves names.

![The history of a repository. Each white box is a commit, named by the start of its hash, and points to its parent. The gray boxes are names: `main` and `feature` are branches, which move on with each new commit, and `HEAD` names the branch checked out; `v1.0.0` is a tag, which stays; `origin/main` is where `main` was on the remote at the last fetch, one commit behind.](figures/commits.svg){#fig-commits}


## A commit is a snapshot, named by its hash {#sec-commits}

A commit holds the whole project, not the changes: every file as it was when the
commit was made. The changes that `git diff` and `git log -p` show are computed
from two snapshots when they are asked for. A commit also holds its author, its
date, its message, and the hash of its parent, and its own hash is computed from
all of these, such as `8b41d07…`, of which the first seven characters usually
suffice. Changing anything, even a word of the message, gives another hash, and
so another commit. Because a commit names its parent, which names its own, one
hash identifies the code together with its whole history: two clones that have
a commit have the same files in it.

Because every commit holds every file, the repository keeps every version of
every file for as long as it exists. A file that does not change is stored once,
so this costs little for code. A dataset of a few gigabytes committed once,
however, stays in every clone, even after the next commit deletes it, and so do
a password and a patient record
([](../../principles/testing.qmd#sec-isolated)). Removing such a file means
rewriting every commit since it was added (@sec-rewrite), and every clone made
in the meantime still holds it.


## What goes in, and what stays out {#sec-ignore}

A repository holds what was written: the code, the configuration, the
documentation, small test data, and the recipes of everything that was made
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-recipe)), such as an environment or lock
file, a Dockerfile, and the scripts that draw the figures. It does not hold what
the recipes make, such as results, built packages, and environments like
`.venv/`, nor what is too large or too confidential for every clone: raw data,
which belong in an archive, and secrets, such as tokens and passwords.

A file `.gitignore` lists patterns of files that Git does not offer to add
(@sec-start). It applies only to untracked files, those never added: a file that
was committed stays tracked, with all its changes, until `git rm --cached`
removes it from the next commit, though not from the history. Large files that
must be versioned with the code, such as reference data that tests read, can go
to Git LFS, which keeps only a pointer to each file in the commits, or to DVC.


## The index is the next commit {#sec-index}

A change passes through three places on its way into the history:

| Place | Holds | Changes with |
|---------------|-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Working tree | The files as you edit them | Editing, `git restore` |
| Index | The snapshot that the next commit will be | `git add`, `git restore --staged` |
| Repository | The commits | `git commit` |

`git add` copies a file as it is now into the index, also called the staging
area, and `git commit` turns the index into a commit. A file changed again after
`git add` goes into the commit as it was when it was added; `git status` then
lists it as staged and as changed. `git diff` shows what `git add` would add,
the difference between the working tree and the index, and `git diff --staged`
what `git commit` would record, the difference between the index and the last
commit. A new file is untracked until it is first added: Git neither records it
nor ever restores it.

The index lets a commit hold less than everything that changed, such as one fix
while another change waits, and `git add -p` adds the changes of a file hunk by
hunk. A commit that does one thing can be reviewed, reverted, and found again
when it changed a result (@sec-atomic).


## A branch is a name that moves {#sec-branches}

A branch is a name for a commit, its tip, and nothing more: a file that holds a
hash. `HEAD` names the branch you are on. A new commit gets the tip as its
parent, and the branch moves on to it, while the other branches stay where they
are. A branch therefore costs nothing to create, and switching to one, with
`git switch`, replaces the files of the working tree with those of its tip.
Uncommitted changes come along, unless the other branch has changed the same
files, in which case Git refuses to switch.

A tag is a name that does not move: `v1.0.0` names the commit of a release for
good. An annotated tag, made with `git tag -a`, also records who made it, when,
and why, as a release should (@sec-tag). Checking out a tag or a commit, with
`git switch --detach v1.0.0`, puts `HEAD` on a commit instead of a branch: in
this detached state, you can look around and run the code, but a new commit
belongs to no branch and drops out of sight when you switch away (@sec-reflog).

Merging joins two lines of history. When the current branch is contained in the
other, `git merge` only moves its name forward, a fast-forward; when both have
commits of their own, it makes a merge commit, with two parents. Where both
changed the same lines, the merge stops with a conflict: Git writes both
versions into the file, between markers, and leaves the choice to you, which
you record with `git add` and finish with `git merge --continue`.


## A clone knows the remote as of the last fetch {#sec-remotes}

A clone holds the whole history and works without the repository it came from.
That repository is its remote, named `origin`, and Git exchanges commits with it
only when told: `git fetch` gets the commits that the remote has and the clone
does not, `git push` sends those the clone has and the remote does not, and
`git pull` fetches and then brings the fetched commits into the current branch.

What a clone knows about the remote is what it learned at the last fetch.
`origin/main` is a remote-tracking branch, the place where `main` was on
`origin` then, not where it is now. `git status` reports "Your branch is up to
date with 'origin/main'" when the branch agrees with this record, even if others
have pushed since; only after `git fetch` does it say how far behind the branch
is.

A push moves a branch of the remote forward, and only forward. If the remote
has commits that yours does not contain, because someone pushed in the
meantime, the push is rejected: fetch their commits, merge them or rebase onto
them (@sec-rewrite), and push again. Tags do not travel with the branches
unless asked to (@sec-tag), and a clone that already has a tag keeps it, without
a word, when the tag is moved on the remote. Never move a tag that others may
have fetched.


## Rewriting history makes new commits {#sec-rewrite}

A commit cannot be changed, only replaced. `git commit --amend` makes a new
commit with the corrections and moves the branch to it, and `git rebase main`
replays the commits of the current branch on top of `main`, one by one, as new
commits with new hashes, so that the history becomes a straight line instead of
a merge. The old commits remain (@sec-reflog), and so does every copy of them in
other clones.

That is harmless for commits that only you have, and confusing for commits that
others have built on: their branches still hold the old commits, and the next
merge brings them back next to their copies. Rewrite only commits that you have
not pushed, or those of a branch of your own, such as the branch of a pull
request; never rewrite `main` or a release, whose hash others may have cited.
The remote rejects a push that would drop commits unless it is forced, and
`git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes` forces it only if every commit
it drops has been on your own branch, so that it cannot overwrite what someone
else pushed in the meantime. `--force-with-lease` alone checks against
`origin/main` as of the last fetch: after a fetch, such as one that an editor
runs in the background, it overwrites the commits that the fetch brought in,
unseen.


## Nothing committed is lost {#sec-reflog}

Git removes a commit only when no name and no entry of the reflog reach it any
more, and then only after two weeks. `git reflog` lists every commit that `HEAD`
has been on, with the command that moved it there; its entries are kept for 90
days, or 30 for commits that the branch no longer contains. A commit lost to
`git reset --hard`, a rebase, a deleted branch, or a detached `HEAD` is found
there and named again with `git branch rescue <commit>`.

What Git cannot give back is what was never committed. `git restore` and
`git reset --hard` overwrite changes in the working tree without asking, and an
untracked file that is deleted is gone. Commit early, on a branch of your own if
need be, and tidy up before sharing (@sec-rewrite).


## A changed working tree is code without a name {#sec-dirty}

A commit names code only if the working tree holds no changes. A result computed
from a working tree with uncommitted changes, and recorded with the hash of the
last commit, claims code that never ran, as does the record of an MLflow run
started from such a tree ([](../tracking/mlflow.qmd#sec-only-what-logged)).
`git describe --tags --always --dirty` prints a name for the state of the
working tree: `v1.2.0` at a tagged commit, `v1.2.0-3-g1a2b3c4` three commits
after the tag, at commit `1a2b3c4`, and `-dirty` at the end when tracked files
have changed. A file that was never added does not count, so a new script that
has not been committed leaves the name clean. `git status --porcelain` lists it,
and prints nothing only for a working tree that matches the commit, apart from
ignored files.

Record the name with every result that counts
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-traceability)), and let workflow code refuse
to start such a run, or at least warn, when `git status --porcelain` prints
anything.


# Working with Git {#sec-usage}

The commands below cover daily work. After most of them, `git status` says where
things stand and what to do next, and `git help <command>` explains any of them.


## Set up {#sec-setup}

```bash
git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.org"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main  # master until Git 3.0
git config --global pull.rebase true         # pull replays unpushed commits
git config --list --show-origin              # every setting, and its file
```

The name and the email go into every commit, and changing them later means
rewriting it; use those under which you publish. `git pull` stops when both the
branch and the remote have new commits, until told whether to merge or rebase.
With `pull.rebase`, it replays the commits you have not pushed on top of those
fetched, which rewrites only commits that nobody else has (@sec-rewrite).


## Start a repository {#sec-start}

```bash
git init                                     # a new repository, here
git clone git@github.com:lab/stationfit.git  # a copy, with all its history
git remote add origin git@github.com:lab/stationfit.git  # for one from init
git remote -v                                # the remotes and their URLs
```

```default
# .gitignore
# What the code makes, and the data it reads
/results/
/data/
# Environments and caches
.venv/
__pycache__/
.snakemake/
# Secrets
.env
```

A pattern that starts with a slash matches only at the top of the repository,
and one that ends with a slash only directories. The repository
`github/gitignore` has templates for many languages and tools.


## Record changes {#sec-record}

```bash
git status                # what changed, what is staged, what is new
git diff                  # the changes not yet staged
git diff --staged         # the changes staged for the next commit
git add src/fit.py        # stage a file as it is now
git add -p                # stage the changes hunk by hunk
git commit -m "Fix the units of the drift rate"
git commit --amend        # replace the last commit, if not yet pushed
git mv fit.py model.py    # rename a file
git rm --cached big.csv   # stop tracking a file, but keep it on disk
```

The first line of a message is its title, of about 50 characters, and the body,
after an empty line, says why the change was made, since the diff already shows
what changed ([](../../principles/documenting.qmd#sec-comments)).


## Atomic commits: one commit, one change {#sec-atomic}

A commit should hold one change and leave the project working: the tests pass
and the workflow runs. A commit that cannot be described in one sentence
without an "and" is two commits. Commit when a step is finished, not when the
day ends or when the editor has saved something.

The rest of Git works on the history that this makes. `git bisect` tests the
commits between a good and a bad one and cannot judge those that do not run
(@sec-bisect); `git revert` takes back one change without taking another along;
a reviewer reads one idea at a time; and the hash of a commit names code that
ran, which is what makes a result traceable
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-traceability)).

What goes into one commit, and what into two:

- **Together**: a change of behavior, its tests, and its documentation
  ([](../../principles/documenting.qmd#sec-docs-as-code)), with the entry in the
  changelog. A reference output that the change moves goes into the same commit,
  and the message says why the numbers moved
  ([](../../principles/testing.qmd#sec-snapshots)).
- **Apart**: refactoring and a change of behavior. A refactoring leaves every
  result as it was, so the tests alone show that it is one; if numbers move in
  it, it was not. A change that moves numbers also goes in a commit of its own,
  so that the difference in a result can be traced to it. A reformatting of
  whole files, finally, buries the real change in `git blame` and `git diff`,
  and goes in a commit of its own as well.

`git add -p` stages the hunks of a commit when the working tree holds more than
one change, and `git diff --staged` shows what the commit will hold. Work in
progress may be committed early, on a branch of your own (@sec-reflog), but
rewrite those commits into atomic ones before they are pushed (@sec-rewrite).


## Look at the history {#sec-history}

```bash
git log --oneline --graph --all  # every branch, a line per commit
git log -p src/fit.py            # the changes to one file
git log -S "0.05" -- src/        # the commits that added or removed a text
git show 8b41d07                 # one commit, with its changes
git show v1.0.0:src/fit.py       # a file as it was in a release
git diff v1.0.0 v1.1.0 -- src/   # what changed between two releases
git blame src/fit.py             # the last commit of every line
```

`git log -S` finds the commit that changed a constant, such as a tolerance or a
default, which is often the fastest way to learn why a result changed between
two versions.


## Branch and merge {#sec-branch}

```bash
git switch -c fix-units   # create a branch and switch to it
git switch main           # switch to a branch
git branch -a             # the branches, with those of the remotes
git merge fix-units       # merge a branch into the current one
git rebase main           # replay the current branch on top of main
git branch -d fix-units   # delete a branch that has been merged
```

When a merge or a rebase stops with a conflict:

```bash
git status                # the files with conflicts
git add src/fit.py        # mark a file as resolved, after editing it
git merge --continue      # or git rebase --continue
git merge --abort         # or git rebase --abort: back to the start
```


## Share {#sec-share}

```bash
git fetch                       # get new commits; changes none of yours
git pull                        # fetch, and bring them into this branch
git push                        # send this branch
git push -u origin fix-units    # the first push of a new branch
git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes  # after a rebase of your own
```

A pull request belongs to GitHub, not to Git: a request to merge one branch into
another, with its changes, a review, and the checks that [](github-actions.qmd)
runs. GitHub's command-line tool, `gh`, opens and merges them:

```bash
gh pr create --fill       # open a pull request for this branch
gh pr checkout 42         # check out the branch of pull request 42
gh pr merge 42 --squash   # merge it as a single commit
```

A squash merge, like a rebase merge, puts new commits on `main`, not those of
the branch, so `git branch -d` afterwards refuses to delete the branch as not
merged; `git branch -D` deletes it.


## Tag a release {#sec-tag}

```bash
git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Version 1.2.0"  # tag the current commit
git push origin v1.2.0                # tags are pushed one by one
git push --follow-tags                # or with the commits they tag
git tag --list                        # every tag
git describe --tags --always --dirty  # the name of the current state
git switch --detach v1.2.0            # check out a release
```

Tag the commit that is released, once its tests pass and the changelog names
the version ([](../../principles/documenting.qmd#sec-changelog)), and never
move the tag afterwards (@sec-remotes). On GitHub, a release is made from a tag;
Zenodo, once connected to the repository, archives every release and gives it a
DOI ([](../../principles/documenting.qmd#sec-cite)).


## Undo {#sec-undo}

| To | Run |
|----------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| Discard the changes to a file | `git restore <file>` |
| Unstage a file, keeping its changes | `git restore --staged <file>` |
| Bring a file back as it was in a release | `git restore --source v1.0.0 <file>` |
| Undo the last commit, not yet pushed, keeping its changes | `git reset --soft HEAD~1` |
| Discard every change since the last commit | `git reset --hard` |
| Undo a pushed commit, with a new commit | `git revert <commit>` |
| Set changes aside, and bring them back | `git stash -u`, then `git stash pop` |
| Find a lost commit, and name it again | `git reflog`, then `git branch rescue <commit>` |

`git restore <file>` and `git reset --hard` discard what was never committed,
which nothing brings back (@sec-reflog). `git stash` without `-u` leaves new
files where they are.


## Find the commit that changed a result {#sec-bisect}

```bash
git bisect start           # start a search
git bisect bad             # the current commit gives the wrong result
git bisect good v1.1.0     # this release gave the right one
git bisect run ./check.sh  # let a script test each commit Git picks
git bisect reset           # back to where the search started
```

`git bisect` halves the commits between a good one and a bad one with each
test, so among a thousand commits it finds the one that changed a result in ten
steps. Without `run`, you test each commit that Git checks out and answer with
`git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`. With `run`, a script tests it: it exits
with 0 when the result is right, with 1 when it is wrong, and with 125 when the
commit cannot be tested, such as when it does not build, which Git then skips.
The script compares the result with its expected value within a tolerance
([](../../principles/testing.qmd#sec-float-tests)), and lies outside the
history, such as in another directory, so that the same check runs on every
commit. The search is fastest on a history of small commits that each work
(@sec-atomic).
